rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's response differs: human deviation precedes divine leading astray, while believers' chosen faith and firmness are followed by God's confirmation and protection from error.
rows.anchor: فرض فيه زيغ منهم ثم إزاغه منه تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reading says God establishes believers in honor and reward through their own firm profession of faith, itself supported by proofs.
rows.anchor: ويقرهم في كرامته وثوابه بالقول الثابت الذي وجد منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i rejects the honor-and-reward reading as an unsupported restriction of the verse.
rows.anchor: وفيه أنه تقييد من غير مقيد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reported reading takes establishment as earthly power, support, and victory, followed by entry into Paradise; the author finds it contextually remote.
rows.anchor: يثبتهم بالتمكين في الأرض والنصرة والغلبة في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast identifies the wrongdoers as disbelievers; God deprives them of guidance and hence of happiness in this life and lasting favor in the next.
rows.anchor: المراد بهم أهل الكفر بالله وبآياته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's will governs the believers' confirmation and disbelievers' misguidance without any obstacle, making believer felicity and disbeliever misery a settled decree.
rows.anchor: فمن القضاء المحتوم سعادة المؤمن وشقاء الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the explicit name Allah where a pronoun could stand magnifies the matter and gives the scene solemnity.
rows.anchor: من وقوع الظاهر موقع المضمر ويدل على فخامة الأمر

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ glosses placing something in a locus as adjacency for bodies or penetration for accidents, and glosses al-bawar as destruction.
rows.anchor: الإحلال وضع الشيء في محل إما بمجاورة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives al-bawar from extreme stagnation that leads to spoilage, paralleling the expression that trade will never perish.
rows.anchor: البوار فرط الكساد ولما كان فرط الكساد يؤدي إلى الفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage concerns leaders of unbelief across earlier communities and this community, who answer God's blessings with ingratitude; its scope is not restricted to Meccan or Quraysh opponents.
rows.anchor: والآية مطلقة لا دليل على تقييدها بكفار مكة أو كفار قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them leaders follows from their ability to make their peoples follow them; their act of exchanging blessing for unbelief means replacing the required gratitude with disbelief, or figuratively turning the blessing itself into disbelief.
rows.anchor: المشعر بكونهم نافذي الكلمة مطاعين في قومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their followers' ruin entails the leaders' own ruin, since they first went astray and then led others astray; Pharaoh is a parallel case.
rows.anchor: ضلوا ثم أضلوا والتبعة تبعة الضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about Hell explains what the abode of ruin is.
rows.anchor: بيان لدار البوار، واحتمال بعضهم أن يكون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some parse Jahannam as an accusative by الاشتغال, estimating that they enter Hell and then repeating the verb with its object pronoun; Tabataba'i rejects this as disfavored and pointless.
rows.anchor: منصوبا بالاشتغال، والتقدير يصلون جهنم يصلونها والجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage is not evidence for a Medinan setting aimed specifically at Quraysh chiefs killed at Badr, since that reading improperly narrows its universal wording.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا يظهر فساد قول من قال إن الآيات مدنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making ships serviceable means enabling people to use them for travel and carrying loads without sinking or resisting movement.
rows.anchor: هو جعلها بحيث تنفعهم في مقاصدهم وهي العبور بأنفسهم وأحمالهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say ship-subjection means God enabled people to build and use ships by inspiring them; Tabataba'i rejects this because subjection ordinarily means making an object serve human purposes.
rows.anchor: تسخيرها لهم هو إقدارهم على صنعتها واستعمالها بإلهامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording names ships before the sea because ships are the clearest marine blessing, even though the sea is the greater blessing.
rows.anchor: لكون الفلك من أوضح النعم البحرية وإن لم تنحصر فيها نعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ship movement is attributed to God's command although wind, steam, and other natural causes operate, because God is the encompassing cause to which every cause leads.
rows.anchor: لكونه تعالى هو السبب المحيط الذي إليه ينتهي كل سبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rivers are flowing waters across the lands made compliant for drinking, washing, cleaning, and sustaining the animals and plants placed at human service.
rows.anchor: وهي المياه الجارية في مختلف أقطار الأرض وتسخيرها هو تذليلها

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains dāʾibayn as continuing motion, and also as a settled custom maintained without interruption; Tabataba'i says the verse is otherwise clear.
rows.anchor: الدأب إدامة السير دأب في السير دأبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questioning is a request addressed to a rational being, unlike the broader category of requesting; need prompted people to express requests verbally, though signs and writing also count literally as questions.
rows.anchor: السؤال هو الطلب ويفارقه أن السؤال إنما يكون ممن يعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every created being depends on God's generosity for existence and continuance, so all beings are inherently asking God to meet their needs whether or not they acknowledge Him or receive every requested thing.
rows.anchor: كان كل من سواه عاكفا على باب جوده سائلا يسأله رفع ما حلت به من حاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intrinsic asking is directed only to God; verbal requests may be addressed to God or other people, but the verse's unrestricted giving shows that every need of humanity as a species is met wholly or partly.
rows.anchor: هذا هو حق السؤال وحقيقته يختص به تعالى لا يتعداه إلى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The species' requests are genuine and directed only to its Lord, so all are answered; individual people may make insincere or misdirected prayers, which explains why a particular person's request can go unmet.
rows.anchor: فجميع أدعيته مستجابة وسؤالاته مؤتاة وحاجاته مقضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition min means that God's gifts are drawn from what people asked for, sometimes wholly and sometimes partly according to wisdom; a partitive reading would wrongly imply every request is only partly granted.
rows.anchor: ابتدائية تفيد أن الذي يؤتيه الله مأخوذ مما سألوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading the phrase as giving both what people ask for and what they do not ask for relies on verbal asking, which Tabataba'i has rejected and finds unsupported by the context.
rows.anchor: وما لم تسألوه وهو مبني على كون المراد بالسؤال هو السؤال اللفظي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interdependent universe and its effects are blessings benefiting one another, beyond enumeration; the singular blessing names the whole genus and conveys abundance without a plural.
rows.anchor: فالجميع نعمه بالنسبة إلى الجميع وهذا أمر لا يحيط به إحصاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity is intensely unjust and ungrateful: people wrong themselves by failing to thank God, or wrong God's blessings by denying them; this explanatory comment follows from human heedlessness of those blessings.
rows.anchor: أي كثير الكفران يظلم نفسه فلا يشكر نعمة الله

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet identified the good tree as a date palm and the uprooted bad tree as a colocynth.
rows.anchor: عن أنس قال أتي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بقناع من بسر فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i says the date-palm identification appears in several Prophetic reports but only applies the parable to that tree; the report's ending conflicts with the next report.
rows.anchor: وهي لا تدل على أزيد من انطباق المثل عليها

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that Companions proposed truffles for the uprooted tree; the Prophet replied that truffles are manna and cure the eye, while ajwa dates are from Paradise and cure poison.
rows.anchor: قعد ناس من أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم فذكروا هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The colocynth too has important medicinal properties, qualifying an inference that the bad-tree comparison requires it to be useless.
rows.anchor: والكلام يجري في الحنظلة فإن لها خواص طبية هامة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits Ali's gloss that ḥīn means six months; Tabataba'i says the same discussion as for the preceding report applies.
rows.anchor: أخرج البيهقي في سننه عن علي قال الحين ستة أشهر

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: In a report from ʿAmr b. Ḥurayth, the Prophet is applied as the tree's root, Ali as its branch, the Imams as its boughs, their knowledge as fruit, and believers as leaves.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أصلها وأمير المؤمنين فرعها والأئمة من ذريتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i treats these identifications as applications, not exclusive meanings, since reports give different correspondences for the root, branch, fruit, and leaves.
rows.anchor: فالرواية من باب التطبيق ومن الدليل عليه اختلاف الروايات في كيفية التطبيق

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu al-Jarud reports from al-Baqir that the bad-tree parable represents the Umayyads; al-Ayyashi transmits a related application to the Prophet's household and their opponents.
rows.anchor: روى أبو الجارود عن أبي جعفر عليه السلام أن هذا - يعني قوله كشجرة خبيثة الخ - مثل بني أمية

rows.speaker: الآلوسي
rows.claim: Al-Alusi cites an Imami interpretation identifying the good tree with Muhammad, Ali, Fatima, and their descendants, and the bad tree with the Umayyads.
rows.anchor: وروى الإمامية وأنت تعرف حالهم عن أبي جعفر رضي الله عنه تفسيرها

rows.speaker: الآلوسي
rows.claim: Al-Alusi cites a report that Quraysh is the blessed tree, then reasons that the Umayyads belong to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وهي الشجرة المباركة التي قال الله تعالى في كتابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if Quraysh is blessed as a whole, that does not make every branch or descendant good; Tabataba'i names Banu Abd al-Dar, Abu Jahl, and Abu Lahab as counterexamples.
rows.anchor: فأي ملازمة بين كون شجرة بحسب أصلها مباركة طيبة وبين كون بعض فروعها

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Ibn Mardaway reports Aisha telling Marwan b. al-Hakam that the Prophet called his father and grandfather the accursed tree mentioned in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: روى ابن مردويه هذا عن عائشة أنها قالت لمروان بن الحكم سمعت رسول الله

rows.speaker: سهل بن ساعد، عبد الله بن عمر، يعلى بن مرة، الحسين بن علي، سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Commentators transmit from these authorities that the Umayyads were the people connected to the vision and accursed tree; Saʿd's report describes them leaping like monkeys on the Prophet's pulpit and the Prophet's grief.
rows.anchor: روى أصحاب التفاسير كالطبري وغيره عن سهل بن ساعد وعبد الله بن عمر

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Ayyashi reports al-Sadiq saying Satan tries to mislead a loyal believer at death from both sides, but God prevents him, illustrating God's confirmation of believers.
rows.anchor: عن صفوان بن مهران عن أبي عبد الله عليه السلام قال الشيطان ليأتي الرجل من أوليائنا

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر، أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from al-Baqir and al-Sadiq describes two angels and Satan questioning the dead: believers affirm Muhammad and rest with a view of Paradise, whereas unbelievers cannot answer and are left to Satan.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله عليه السلام قالا إذا وضع الرجل في قبره

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Baraʾ b. ʿAzib reports the Prophet saying that a Muslim questioned in the grave testifies that none is god but God and Muhammad is God's messenger, which is the verse's firm word.
rows.anchor: المسلم إذا سئل في القبر يشهد أن لا إله إلا الله وأن محمدا رسول الله

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid al-Khudri reports the Prophet explaining that the verse's hereafter refers to the grave.
rows.anchor: أخرج الطبراني في الأوسط وابن مردويه عن أبي سعيد الخدري سمعت رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many Sunni and Shiʿi reports describe the grave questioning by Munkar and Nakir and the believer's firmness versus the disbeliever's misguidance, often citing this verse.
rows.anchor: وهناك روايات كثيرة من طرق الشيعة وأهل السنة وردت في تفصيل سؤال القبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports take the hereafter as the grave because steadfastness implies a setting where one might stumble; more broadly, believers remain established by God in both the intermediate realm and resurrection, so Tabataba'i treats the reports as applications.
rows.anchor: والأولى أخذ الروايات من قبيل التطبيق

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Al-Ayyashi reports Ali's application of God's blessing to the people through whom God blessed His servants: the Prophet's household.
rows.anchor: قال نحن نعمة الله التي أنعم الله بها على العباد

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali identifies the two most wicked Quraysh groups as Banu Umayya and Banu al-Mughira; al-Ayyashi and al-Durr transmit this attribution.
rows.anchor: قال هما الأفجران من قريش بنو أمية وبنو المغيرة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In a report transmitted through several Sunni collections, Ali names Banu al-Mughira and Banu Umayya as those who exchanged God's blessing for disbelief; Badr eliminated the former, while the latter were reprieved.
rows.anchor: قال هما الأفجران من قريش بنو أمية وبنو المغيرة فأما بنو المغيره فقطع الله دابرهم

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar gives the same identification, saying Banu al-Mughira were dealt with at Badr and Banu Umayya were allowed respite.
rows.anchor: أخرج البخاري في تاريخه وابن جرير وابن المنذر وابن مردويه عن عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas tells Umar that the two groups were the most wicked Quraysh clans, identifying Banu al-Mughira as his maternal uncles and Banu Umayya as Umar's paternal uncles.
rows.anchor: وفيه أخرج ابن مردويه عن ابن عباس أنه قال لعمر يا أمير المؤمنين

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq reports that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali about the verse and Ali answered that Quraysh changed God's blessing into disbelief and denied His Prophet at Badr; varying applications show these are not occasions of revelation.
rows.anchor: قال تلك قريش بدلوا نعمة الله كفرا وكذبوا نبيه يوم بدر

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: Al-Kafi reports that when al-Sajjad recited the verse on counting blessings, he praised God for making recognition of blessings consist in admitting one's inability to know them, and treating that admission as gratitude.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن محمد عن بعض أصحابه رفعه قال كان على بن الحسين عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding description means they inwardly know truth but persist in rejecting it from arrogance, desire, and self-satisfaction, as in the cited examples.
rows.anchor: فاتباعهم هوى أنفسهم ومضيهم على ما هم عليه من الإعراض عن الحق عنادا واستكبارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The losers are those who deny God's signs in the world and themselves, as well as the signs and miracles brought by prophets; denying encounter with God means rejecting return to Him and resurrection, a trait of idolaters.
rows.anchor: آياته تعالى في الآفاق والأنفس وما يأتي به الأنبياء والرسل من المعجزات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their deeds are void because they neither act for God nor seek the next life's reward and happiness, and remembrance of Judgment does not motivate them.
rows.anchor: أنهم لا يعملون عملا لوجه الله ولا يريدون ثواب الدار الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The weighing of deeds at Judgment measures the heaviness of good deeds; because these people's deeds are null, they have no weight, as shown by the cited passage.
rows.anchor: والوزن يوم القيامة بثقل الحسنات على ما يدل عليه قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative summarizes their described condition; their recompense is Hell, and mockery of God's signs and messengers adds further disbelief to their initial disbelief.
rows.anchor: في معنى بما كفروا وازدادوا كفرا باستهزاء آياتي ورسلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Firdaws is variously described as a garden in Greek, a vineyard in Nabataean or Syriac, Paradise in Abyssinian, or in Arabic a densely wooded garden, usually with vines; it is used as masculine or feminine.
rows.anchor: الفردوس يذكر ويؤنث قيل هي البستان بالرومية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer from Hell and Paradise each being called a lodging that further punishment and reward remain undescribed; the discussion begins to cite possible supporting examples.
rows.anchor: وقد استفاد بعضهم من عده جنات الفردوس نزلا وقد عد سابقا جهنم للكافرين نزلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah recounts four episodes of Moses: his call and mission against Pharaoh, the confrontation and signs, the exodus and Pharaoh's drowning, and the calf and Samiri; this passage tells the first episode.
rows.anchor: وقد تعرضت الآيات التي نقلناها للفصل الأول منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story connects to the preceding passage by recalling monotheism and warning of punishment: it opens with revelation of God's oneness and ends by affirming it, echoing the surah's opening reminder and closing divine names.
rows.anchor: ووجه اتصال القصة بما قبلها أنها تذكره بالتوحيد ووعيد بالعذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question Have you heard the story of Moses? is a rhetorical request for confirmation, and ḥadīth means a story.
rows.anchor: الإستفهام للتقرير والحديث، القصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makath means stay; ānasa means seeing or finding, strongly perceiving something familiar; qabas is a flame carried on a stick, and hudā means guidance or a guide.
rows.anchor: المكث اللبث، والإيناس إبصار الشيء أو وجدانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was returning from Midian toward Egypt on a cold dark night with his family near Tuwa in Sinai; they had lost the road, so he went toward the fire to ask directions or bring back a flame for warmth.
rows.anchor: كان في منصرفه من مدين إلى مصر ومعه أهله وهم بالقرب من وادي طوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His instruction to stay indicates others were with his family; the emphatic report that he alone perceived a fire indicates that the others did not see it, and an omitted clause means he would go and return with flame or a guide.
rows.anchor: مع ما يشتمل عليه من التأكيد والتعبير بالإيناس دلالة على أنه إنما رآها هو وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tuwa is a valley at Sinai's Mount Tur, also called the sacred valley; removing the sandals shows respect for the consecrated place of divine presence and intimate converse.
rows.anchor: وهذه التسمية والتوصيف هي الدليل على أن أمره بخلع النعلين إنما هو لاحترام الوادي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقدماء المفسرين
rows.claim: Some who accept Pharaoh's faith at drowning argue that God's laʿalla must occur, so one of remembrance or fear—and thus salvation—was guaranteed.
rows.anchor: من الله واجب الوقوع كما نسب إلى ابن عباس وقدماء المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i rejects that premise: laʿalla expresses contextual expectation, not an inevitable outcome in God's speech, since God is beyond ignorance or hopefulness.
rows.anchor: ولا تدل عسى ولعل في كلامه تعالى إلا على ما يدل عليه في كلام غيره

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the reason for sending Moses to Pharaoh despite knowing he would not believe is unknowable, so one must submit and avoid objection; Tabataba'i calls this strange.
rows.anchor: وقال الإمام الرازي في تفسيره أنه لا يعلم سر إرساله تعالى إلى فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For free-choice proponents, command and invitation remain valid because response is possible relative to the human agent, even if the full combination of external causes makes compliance impossible.
rows.anchor: والأمر لا يتعلق بالفعل من حيث حاله بالقياس إلى جميع أجزاء علته التامة

rows.speaker: المجبرة
rows.claim: Determinists such as al-Razi answer that commands are merely formal, serving to complete the proof and remove excuses; Tabataba'i says their determinism makes the same problem apply to all obligations.
rows.anchor: بأن التكليف صوري يترتب عليه تمام الحجة وقطع المعذرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even when some hearers refuse truth, genuine invitation benefits some by perfecting felicity and others by perfecting misery, so sending the messengers is not pointless.
rows.anchor: الدعوة الحقة كما تؤثر أثرها في قوم بتكميلهم في جانب السعادة

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Faqih reports al-Sadiq explaining that Moses' sandals were made from the hide of a dead donkey; al-Qummi and Sunni transmitters also report this, while the context points to reverence for the place.
rows.anchor: وفي الفقيه سئل الصادق عليه السلام عن قول الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ reports that establishing prayer for God's remembrance means praying whenever one recalls an owed prayer, whether or not it is its appointed time; this is also attributed to al-Baqir.
rows.anchor: قيل معناه أقم الصلاة متى ذكرت أن عليك صلاة كنت في وقتها أم لم تكن

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports the Prophet saying that whoever forgets a prayer should perform it upon remembering, with no expiation other than that; Muslim records the report and other Sunni and Shiʿi routes transmit it.
rows.anchor: من نسي صلاة فليصلها إذا ذكرها لا كفارة لها غير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to read Akādu ukh fīhā as I almost conceal it from Myself; the same reading is attributed to Ubayy and reported from al-Sadiq.
rows.anchor: روى عن ابن عباس { أكاد أخفيها عن نفسي

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت عميس
rows.claim: Asmaʾ bint ʿUmays reports seeing the Prophet facing Mount Thabir and praying for Ali as his brother and minister, asking God to strengthen and associate him in his affair, as Moses had prayed.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن مردويه والخطيب وابن عساكر عن أسماء بنت عميس قالت رأيت

rows.speaker: الآلوسي
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the Prophet's request that Ali share in his affair can only mean guidance and calling to truth, not prophethood, and cannot establish Ali's immediate succession; he compares the Tabuk deputyship report.
rows.anchor: لا يخفى أنه يتعين هنا حمل الأمر على أمر الإرشاد والدعوة إلى الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i leaves the succession debate aside and examines what share in the Prophet's affair means; he regards the report as sound and supported by the widely transmitted hadith of al-Manzila.
rows.anchor: فالبحث فيه خارج عن غرض الكتاب وإنما نبحث عن المراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sharing in the Prophet's affair cannot mean prophethood, which the al-Manzila hadith explicitly excludes, or generic guidance and preaching, which all Muslims share and the possessive wording makes nonexclusive.
rows.anchor: وليس المراد بالأمر هو مطلق الإرشاد والدعوة إلى الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rather it means first transmission of revelation and its prophetic effects, including binding authority; Moses' request for Aaron's support means clarifying, elaborating, and conveying some revelation, and this is the Prophet's intended meaning for Ali too.
rows.anchor: نعم التبليغ الابتدائي وهو تبليغ الوحي لأول مرة أمر يختص بالنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion connects the interpretation to the Prophet sending Ali with the opening verses of al-Tawba after removing Abu Bakr, based on revelation that only the Prophet or a man from him could convey them.
rows.anchor: لا يبلغها عنك إلا أنت أو رجل منك

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Qummi transmits from al-Baqir that Pharaoh killed Israelite boys after learning a prophesied Moses would destroy him, separating and imprisoning the men while his wives monitored the women.
rows.anchor: كان فرعون قد وكل بنساء بني إسرائيل نساءه من القبط يحفظنهن

rows.speaker: أم موسى
rows.claim: The birth narrative says Moses' mother feared that her newborn would be killed, but God's favor made the Coptic woman assigned to watch her feel compassion; the infant's beauty manifested the love God placed on him.
rows.anchor: وكان موسى لا يراه أحد إلا أحبه وهو قول الله

rows.speaker: موسى بن جعفر
rows.claim: In a report through Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, al-Kazim explains speaking gently as addressing Pharaoh by his kunya, Abu Musʿab, whose name was al-Walid b. Musʿab.
rows.anchor: أي كنياه وقولا له يا أبا مصعب وكان كنية فرعون أبا مصعب الوليد بن مصعب

rows.speaker: موسى بن جعفر
rows.claim: The same report says laʿalla was phrased to make Moses more eager to go, although God knew Pharaoh would not remember or fear until drowning; Pharaoh's late profession was rejected.
rows.anchor: وقد علم الله عز وجل أن فرعون لا يتذكر ولا يخشى إلا عند رؤية البأس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i says using a kunya is only one example of gentle speech, not its sole form, and notes that the report's second portion is also transmitted in al-Kafi.
rows.anchor: وتفسير القول اللين بالتكنية من قبيل ذكر بعض المصاديق لضرورة أنه لا ينحصر فيه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report through ʿAdi b. Hatim from Ali supports Tabataba'i's reading that laʿalla in the verse expresses hope or expectation.
rows.anchor: عن علي عليه السلام وفيه تأييد ما قدمنا أن { لعل } مستعملة في الآية للترجي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from play to pastime develops the argument: amusement relieves a need, so God cannot be amused by creation, which belongs to Him and cannot supply what He lacks.
rows.anchor: وتلهيه تعالى بشيء من خلقه محال لأن اللهو لا يتم لهوا إلا برفع حاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God took amusement, it would have to arise from His own essence rather than creation, an impossible supposition; the verse's if and its closing phrase reinforce the impossibility.
rows.anchor: بل وجب أن يكون بأمر غير خارج من ذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since creation is not purposeless play, it has an end: return to God and judgment require prophets to guide people toward accountable belief and action, and divine punishment can vindicate truth.
rows.anchor: فالمعاد هو الغرض من الخلقة الموجب للنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadhf is throwing at a distance, damgh is a head wound reaching the brain, and zahūq is perishing; truth has real stability, whereas falsehood only resembles truth, as water differs from a mirage.
rows.anchor: والدمغ - على ما في مجمع البيان - شج الرأس حتى يبلغ الدماغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an treats factual beliefs and the afterlife as truth, worldly possessions and secondary causes as falsehood, and God alone as absolute truth.
rows.anchor: وعد الحياة الآخرة حقا والحياة الدنيا بجميع ما يراه الإنسان لنفسه فيها ويسعى له سعيه من ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falsehood arises as a deficiency relative to something more complete, and is related to God only by permission; a salt flat that appears like water illustrates a merely imagined mirage.
rows.anchor: فليس ينتسب إليه بالاستقامة وإنما هو لازم نقص بعض الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All existence has some admixture of falsehood, while God is pure truth; the created order's mixture is illustrated by the rainwater and foam parable.
rows.anchor: أن الله هو الحق النور 24، ويظهر أيضا أن الخلقة على ما فيها من النظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's continuing practice is to give falsehood time, then cast truth upon it so that it vanishes; truth's beliefs, perfection, and prophetic victory endure even against few followers or severe opposition.
rows.anchor: وقد جرت سنة الله تعالى أن يمهل الباطل حتى إذا اعترض الحق ليبطله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated verb signals an ongoing law, truth's casting on falsehood signals superiority, and the sudden vanishing signals a surprising reversal; the rule is unrestricted across belief, practice, and creation.
rows.anchor: المفيد للاستمرار دلالة على كونه سنة جارية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret the verse as saying that God sets earnestness, as a kind of truth, against amusement, but Tabataba'i rejects this because it assumes divine amusement which the preceding passage denied.
rows.anchor: لكنا لا نريد اتخاذ اللهو بل شأننا أن نغلب الحق الذي من جملته الجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is directed at those who deny resurrection and prophethood; return to God means God continuously purifies truth from whatever obscures it until only the absolute truth remains.
rows.anchor: وعيد للناس المنكرين للمعاد والنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse denies other gods whose divinity governs heaven and earth, not rival creators, since no one claims there are multiple independent creators; divine presence in both realms means authority over them, not residence.
rows.anchor: والمراد بكون الإله في السماء والأرض تعلق ألوهيته بالسماء والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If multiple gods existed, their distinct essences would yield conflicting governance and corrupt the heavens and earth; the harmonious, unified order proves the world's one God.
rows.anchor: لكن النظام الجاري نظام واحد متلائم الأجزاء في غاياتها

rows.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
rows.claim: A common explanation says God is not questioned because He acts only with a justified benefit as the absolutely wise, whereas humans may act rightly or wrongly and can be held accountable.
rows.anchor: هذا ما ذكره جماعة من المفسرين في توجيه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i accepts this explanation as sound in general but says the verse's wording does not establish that this is its intended meaning.
rows.anchor: لكن يبقى عليه أمران الأمر الأول أن الآية مطلقة لا دليل فيها من جهة اللفظ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another interpretation says divine acts have no external purpose, since a purpose would complete or benefit God; God's own essence is the end of His acts, like generosity that eventually acts for itself.
rows.anchor: وجه بعضهم عدم السؤال بأنه مبني على كون أفعال الله لا تعلل بالأغراض

rows.speaker: بعض آخر
rows.claim: A further view attributes the lack of questioning to God's majesty and power, which make all others too low to challenge Him; Tabataba'i rejects this as mere fear of a tyrant, not intrinsic perfection of action.
rows.anchor: عظمته تعالى وكبرياءه وعزته وبهاءة تقهر كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabataba'i says the Qur'an depicts divine action as free of defect and deficiency, not merely beyond challenge because no one dares question a ruler's power.
rows.anchor: عدم السؤال من جهة أن ليس هناك من يتمكن من سؤاله اتقاء من قهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wisdom describes an agent through the match between action and the real order; human actions imitate an external order using prior knowledge, but God's act is the actual external order and is itself wisdom, not a response to a higher purpose.
rows.anchor: وأما الفعل الذي هو نفس الخارج وهو فعل الله سبحانه فهو نفس الحكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other agents can be asked to justify why they acted and identify the motivating benefit, but God has no external order above His act to which it must conform and no higher standard beyond His own action.
rows.anchor: وأما هو سبحانه فلا مورد للسؤال عن فعله إذ فعله نفس النظام الخارجي

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some posit a prior detailed acquired knowledge in God of things that already have their own pre-creation reality, potentials, and benefits, after which He brings them into existence; Tabataba'i rejects the account.
rows.anchor: وأما ما ذكره بعضهم أن له تعالى علما تفصيليا بالأشياء قبل إيجادها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects that account because divine knowledge is presential rather than acquired, nonexistent things cannot possess prior thingness or reality, and potentials and benefits presuppose actual external states and relative deficiency.
rows.anchor: بل هو علم حضوري وليس هو بتابع للمعلوم بل الأمر بالعكس

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Al-Maḥasin transmits a raised report from Yunus quoting al-Sadiq: whenever falsehood confronts truth, truth overcomes it; this is the meaning of the verse.
rows.anchor: عن يونس رفعه قال قال أبو عبد الله عليه السلام ليس من باطل يقوم بإزاء حق إلا غلب الحق الباطل

rows.speaker: أيوب بن الحر
rows.claim: A second al-Sadiq report says truth comes to every person and breaks the heart of whoever accepts or leaves it; Tabataba'i says both reports generalize the verse.
rows.anchor: عن أيوب بن الحر قال قال أبو عبد الله عليه السلام يا أيوب ما من أحد إلا وقد يرد عليه الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two reports apply the verse broadly rather than limiting it to one historical contest.
rows.anchor: والروايتان مبنيتان على تعميم الآية

rows.speaker: الرضا
rows.claim: In a report about Harut and Marut, al-Rida says angels are protected by God's grace from disbelief and disgraceful acts, citing verses that describe their obedience and uninterrupted worship.
rows.anchor: إن الملائكة معصومون محفوظون عن الكفر والقبائح بألطاف الله تعالى
